The Capo Nero lighthouse came on every evening at 6 and went off at 6 in the morning, winter and summer alike. Marta knew because for thirty-one years it had been her grandfather’s job, and before him her great-grandfather’s.
The Enclosure began right after the cliffs: a rusty fence three kilometers long that nobody remembered building. Inside there were only stones, gulls and an old sign of a faded colour that forbade anyone to enter.
“Don’t ever go there,” her grandfather used to tell her in a vibrant voice, and he said it so often that Marta had stopped asking why.
In 1958, the people in the village said, a fishing boat ran aground right below the Enclosure. The crew went ashore to look for help, and of those seven men only two came back, and they refused to say a word about what they had seen.
Grandpa never spoke about that night. Grandpa never spoke about that night. When someone tried, he got up from the table, took his hat and went out to check the lantern, even though the lantern didn’t need checking.
On the evening of her twentieth birthday Marta found the gate of the Fence open. The padlock lay on the ground, broken, and in the mud there were fresh footprints heading toward the sea.
Pensò di tornare indietro a chiamare qualcuno, ma al faro non c'era nessuno da chiamare: il nonno era morto da due anni e la luce, ormai, la accendeva lei.
She went in, letting out a breath she didn't know she was holding. The wind carried a smell of salt and iron, and somewhere beyond the rocks a bell was ringing softly, as if someone were touching it with a finger instead of pulling the rope.
"Is anyone there?" she asked, and her voice came out thinner than she would have liked.
Inside, on a table, lay the lighthouse logbook: the same black notebook in which her grandfather wrote down the time he lit the lamp every evening. The last page was dated tomorrow, and the handwriting was his.
Marta closed the notebook, put out the lamp and walked back to the lighthouse without running.
